## 1. Core Mental Model

Every guess you submit returns a **rank** against each currently‑unsolved target in the puzzle: `0` = the exact sentence‑form answer, smaller positive numbers = closer, `MISS` = outside whatever neighborhood the game stores for that target. The displayed **clue** for a target only updates when a guess *strictly improves* on the best rank seen so far for it — so track ranks yourself; a guess that doesn't improve the display still taught you something (e.g., that a whole branch of vocabulary is wrong) and should not be repeated.

Treat the rank you get back as evidence about a **general-purpose distributional similarity space** over French vocabulary — the kind that clusters words which occur in similar contexts across broad text — not a hand-curated synonym list for this one sentence. In that kind of space, inflectional siblings of the true answer, true synonyms, antonyms on a shared scale, words from a different part of speech that share the same underlying concept, and words that merely share a topic/category all cluster close together, sometimes indistinguishably by rank alone. **A good rank tells you which direction you're pointed in far more reliably than it tells you which specific relationship you've found.** Section 4 turns this into concrete rules.

Because guesses are broadcast to *every* unsolved target at once, there is no such thing as "wasting" a guess by aiming at the wrong target — the only real waste is a guess you've already tried, or one so generic it teaches you nothing.

---

## 2. Parse Every Blank Before You Guess

You are only ever given the sentence text (with blanks) and, per target, one free starting clue word plus its rank. Nothing else (part of speech, gender, register, rarity) is handed to you directly — derive all of it yourself from the visible sentence, every time.

### 2.1 Identify the grammatical role of each blank

Work through the sentence and classify each blank using visible anchors:

| Visible pattern around the blank | Likely role | How to resolve it |
|---|---|---|
| Determiner/possessive/demonstrative immediately before the blank (or one word before, skipping a blank/visible noun) | The blank (or the word it precedes) is a **noun** | The determiner fixes gender/number: `le/un/ce` → masc.sg; `la/une/cette` → fem.sg; `les/des/ces` → plural; `l'` → singular, gender ambiguous (need another anchor or general knowledge); possessives (`son/sa/ses`, `leur/leurs`) agree with the **noun they attach to**, not with the possessor — don't infer possessor gender from them |
| Blank directly after a (visible or blank) noun, not starting a new clause | **Adjective** agreeing with that noun | When two nouns are present in the sentence, the adjective attaches to whichever noun is textually **adjacent** to it — this is not always the grammatical subject. In this sentence family, target adjectives are essentially always **post-nominal**; if a blank sits immediately *before* a bare noun, reconsider whether it's really an adjective slot before defaulting to one |
| Blank following a modal/volitional verb (want/must/dare/seem to), a "finish by," "continue," "cease/stop," "try/struggle," "swear/promise/refuse," "force/oblige (à)," a perception verb (watch/listen/see/hear) plus its object, a causative "make X do Y," or "came to do X" | **Verb, and it will be the bare infinitive** — see §3.1, this is the single most reliable structural rule available | Convert directly to infinitive; never guess a conjugated form here |
| A perception-verb construction | verb-then-object or object-then-verb are **both** grammatical word orders in French | Don't assume the noun immediately touching such a verb is automatically its object rather than the infinitive, or vice versa — check meaning |
| Single-word blank immediately after an infinitive verb | **Adverb**, usually a manner adverb | — |
| Single-word blank sitting *between* a "begin/continue/cease"-type conjugated verb and a following linking preposition + infinitive (rather than after the infinitive itself) | Still an **adverb**, but modifying the *onset/frequency/suddenness* of the whole action, not the manner of the embedded verb | Bias candidates toward frequency/suddenness vocabulary rather than pure manner adverbs for this specific configuration |
| Blank at the very start of the sentence, closed off by a comma, before any subject appears | A **fronted past participle used adjectivally**, agreeing with a subject/pronoun that appears *later* in the same sentence | The whole sentence is visible at once — look ahead to that pronoun immediately; there is no real ambiguity |
| Blank inside a prepositional phrase (e.g., "a smell of ___," "the weariness of ___") | **Noun**, object of that preposition | Often carries an abstract or material flavor |

Two nouns and only one adjective (or other combinations outside the common noun/adjective/verb-infinitive/adverb inventory) can occur — don't assume the puzzle only ever uses one fixed template; re-parse from scratch every time rather than pattern-matching to what you've seen before.

### 2.2 Build a register/domain prior

Before brainstorming candidates, read the sentence's imagery once and form a soft prior: a concrete, sensory, physical scene calls for everyday tangible vocabulary; an interior, emotional, or relational scene calls for abstract vocabulary; ornate or old-fashioned phrasing calls for a **higher, more literary register** than casual spoken French — this corpus rewards a broad, sometimes rare vocabulary, not just textbook-basic words. Use this prior to steer brainstorming, not to filter out anything.

---

## 3. Exact-Form Requirements

A guess only scores `0` if it matches the sentence's exact inflected surface form — spelling, accents, elision, and agreement all matter. You can and should test many exploratory words along the way regardless of form; this section is about what the *final, correct* guess must look like once you've located the right concept.

### 3.1 Verb slots take the bare infinitive — treat this as a near-absolute rule

Whenever a blank is structurally a verb (per §2.1), submit the **infinitive**, never a conjugated or participial form, regardless of the surrounding tense or construction. If a strong-ranking neighbor surfaces in conjugated or participial shape, convert it immediately rather than guessing that shape directly — it will not register as solved and wastes a turn you don't need.

**Recognizing the infinitive behind a conjugated/participial shape:**

| You infer or observe (conjugated/participial shape) | Convert to infinitive |
|---|---|
| Regular `-er` verb: `-ant` present participle, or any personal ending (`-e/-es/-ons/-ez/-ent/-ait/-era`...) | strip back to `-er` |
| Regular `-ir` (finir-type) verb: forms containing `-iss-` (`-issant, -issons, -issez, -issait`) | strip back to `-ir` |
| Short-stem `-ir` verb, no `-iss-` (partir/dormir/sortir/servir family) | recognize the short stem, infinitive ends `-ir` |
| Forms like *boit/bois/buvant/bu* | boire (and any prefixed relative) |
| Forms like *coud/couds/cousant/cousu* | coudre (recoudre, découdre…) |
| Forms like *moud/mouds/moulant/moulu* | moudre |
| Forms like *conclut/conclus/concluant* | conclure |
| Forms like *suit/suis/suivant* | suivre (poursuivre…) |
| Forms like *prend/prends/prenant* | prendre (apprendre, comprendre, surprendre…) |
| Forms like *met/mets/mettant* | mettre (permettre, promettre, remettre…) |
| Forms like *vit/vis/vivant* | vivre |
| Forms like *écrit/écris/écrivant* | écrire (décrire, inscrire…) |
| Forms like *croit/crois/croyant* | croire |
| Forms like *peint/peins/peignant*, *craint/craignant*, *joint/joignant* | peindre / craindre / joindre (repeindre, etc.) |
| Forms like *naît/naissant*, *connaît/connaissant* | naître / connaître |
| Forms like *conduit/conduis/conduisant* | conduire (produire, traduire…) |
| Forms like *court/cours/courant* | courir (parcourir, secourir, accourir…) |
| Forms like *rit/ris/riant* | rire (sourire) |
| High-frequency irregulars (*fait, dit, va/vais, est/sont, a/ont, sait, peut, veut, vient, tient, voit, doit, meurt*…) | faire, dire, aller, être, avoir, savoir, pouvoir, vouloir, venir(+devenir/revenir/parvenir), tenir(+obtenir/maintenir/soutenir), voir(+revoir/prévoir), devoir, mourir |
| Any of the above with a prefix (*re-, dé-, sur-, sous-, entre-, contre-*…) attached | identify the base verb's infinitive, then reapply the same prefix |

### 3.2 Adjective agreement

Resolve gender/number from every visible anchor simultaneously (determiner, the noun's own known gender, later pronouns, possessive-marked nouns). Two traps:

- **Epicene adjectives** (already end the same way in masculine and feminine — typically forms ending in `-e`, `-iste`, `-able/-ible`, `-ique`, `-aire`, or certain consonant+e endings, e.g. adjectives like *facile, calme, riche, jeune, rapide*): they don't change spelling with gender. Don't burn a guess "flipping gender" on one of these.
- **Participle-shaped adjectives**: a past-participle-looking word (typical endings `-é/-ée`, `-i/-ie`, `-u/-ue`, or an irregular participle) or a present-participle-looking word (`-ant/-ante`) can be functioning as a plain descriptive adjective agreeing with a noun/subject. If the blank's grammatical role (per §2.1) is "describes a noun," keep it as that agreeing adjective/participle form — do **not** reflexively convert it to an infinitive just because it looks verb-derived.

Once you've confirmed the right lemma via a strong rank but are unsure which agreement variant the sentence needs, it's a legitimate and cheap tactic to **directly test the 2–4 plausible agreement forms** (masc/fem, singular/plural) — only the correct one scores `0`, and the others will typically still rank very close, confirming you have the right concept while you converge on the right form.

### 3.3 Adverb formation

Standard rule: feminine singular adjective + `-ment`. Key exceptions to keep active:
- Adjectives ending `-ant`/`-ent` → `-amment`/`-emment` (e.g. a pattern like *patient→patiemment*, *prudent→prudemment*).
- Adjectives already ending in a vowel take `-ment` directly on the masculine form (no extra `e`).
- Irregulars: *bref→brièvement*, *gentil→gentiment*, *bon→bien*, *mauvais→mal*.
- A whole class of adverbs are **closed-class function words**, not built from any adjective at all (frequency/time words meaning often/rarely/sometimes/always/still/already/soon/late/early/again/inside/outside/for-a-long-time/henceforth, etc.) — recognize and recall these directly rather than trying to morphologically derive them.

### 3.4 Number and spelling discipline

Default expectation is **singular** targets; still, always confirm via the determiner and any verb/pronoun agreement rather than assuming — plural is possible whenever `les/des` or plural agreement appears. Accents and elision are load-bearing for an exact match (a missing accent or wrong ending is a miss, not a near-miss) — proofread every submission. Standard hyphenated compounds are valid single-guess vocabulary items when that's the natural dictionary form.

---

## 4. How to Read Rank Feedback (the embedding-space laws)

A rank number by itself conflates several very different relationships to the true answer. Roughly, in descending order of how often a *very close* rank turns out to reflect each relationship:

1. **An inflectional/conjugational sibling of the same lemma** (plural↔singular, masc↔fem, a conjugated/participial form of a verb you need as an infinitive) — **roughly half** of very-close hits. Fix this with grammar (§3), don't hunt for a different word.
2. **A true near-synonym of a different lemma** — a large share of the remainder. Anchor a synonym-ring search here.
3. **An antonym on a shared scalar/bipolar dimension** — a small but real and *recurring* minority (common enough that you should always sanity-check for it, roughly on the order of one in fifteen-to-twenty very-close hits). See §4.2.
4. **A cross-part-of-speech derivational relative** sharing the same root/concept as the answer but not its required part of speech — a modest minority. Extract the concept, re-express it in the part of speech the blank actually requires.
5. **A same-category neighbor or fixed-collocation partner** — the remainder. You've found the right neighborhood or the right habitual partner-word, not a form of the answer itself; enumerate other members of that category, or the word that habitually accompanies it.

**Operational consequence:** on any strong rank (roughly single digits), pause for one second and ask "does this word's literal meaning actually fit the sentence's meaning and polarity?" before treating it as nearly solved.

### 4.1 Rank-tier interpretation

| Rank observed | What it most likely means | What to do next |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Solved | Stop guessing this target; immediately use the revealed word as fresh context for the rest (§6) |
| 1–3 | Sibling (~half) / synonym (large share) / **antonym (check!)** / wrong-POS relative | Sanity-check fit and polarity first, then derive the grammatically correct form of the right lemma, or flip polarity, or re-express in the right part of speech |
| 4–15 | Strong synonym or close family | Brainstorm several tighter synonyms/collocates in the same register; try agreement variants |
| 15–50 | Right general concept, wrong specific word | Widen the synonym ring; try more specific hyponyms/instances of the concept |
| 50–100 | Plausible but not yet confirmed | Keep varying within the thematic zone; treat a further drop under ~15 as real confirmation |
| Roughly the same band as your starting clue's rank | Domain-level relatedness only (see §5) — not "close" in a meaning sense | Try different specific words within the topic, or reconsider the topic itself |
| Hundreds to low thousands | Weak thematic echo | Low priority; a guess or two more at most before abandoning this branch |
| Deep into the thousands | Still technically inside the stored neighborhood, but functionally uninformative | Don't chase fine differences here; treat like a soft MISS |
| MISS | Outside the stored neighborhood entirely | Strong signal you're on the wrong branch — see §9 pivot tests |

### 4.2 The antonym mirage (treat as a standing law, not a corner case)

Scalar dimensions — temperature, size, speed, weight, timing, fullness/satiation, cleanliness, hardness, skill, effort, intent, precision, moral valence, direction — are encoded by nearly identical surrounding contexts for both poles ("the water is hot/cold," "he acted quickly/slowly"), so the two poles routinely sit closer to each other than either sits to a true synonym. **Whenever a target clearly lives on such a scale, deliberately consider testing the opposite pole as a diagnostic move**: a great rank there confirms you've found the right *axis* even if it's the wrong *pole*, and the sentence itself will almost always tell you trivially which pole is actually wanted once you know the axis. Never treat a rank 1–3 hit on an obvious antonym as "nearly solved" — flip it and submit the other pole directly instead of iterating morphology on the wrong word.

### 4.3 The starting-clue band reflects topic, not synonymy

Because the free starting clue's rank is drawn from a narrow, fixed handicap band regardless of the target, words occupying that band typically reflect **broad domain, function, or category kinship** rather than tight meaning-equivalence — sometimes even a "same function, different/opposite physical direction or location" relationship, or a "typical material/tool/associated item" relationship, rather than anything a bilingual dictionary would call a synonym. Read the clue as a compass pointing at a *field* (a trade, a landscape type, a material category, an emotional register, a domestic space, etc.), then pick the specific word that fits the **sentence itself**, not the clue's literal dictionary meaning.

### 4.4 Cross-part-of-speech drift

Words from a different part of speech than the blank requires routinely surface as strong neighbors because they share the same underlying narrative concept (a noun and the verb built from its root; an adverb and the adjective it derives from; an adverb and a verb sharing a semantic field like "earliness" or "interiority"). Don't discard a strong-but-wrong-POS neighbor — extract the shared concept and re-encode it yourself in the part of speech the blank actually needs.

### 4.5 Polysemy contamination — the most dangerous, most recoverable trap

A common word inherits neighbor structure from **every** sense it has, including senses totally irrelevant to this sentence (a concrete/literal sense clashing with a technical, financial, figurative, or otherwise unrelated dominant sense of the same spelling). This can show up as a misleadingly unrelated starting clue, or even as an unexpectedly great rank on a guess that reflects the wrong sense entirely.

**Diagnostic:** if the starting clue's plain meaning has nothing sensible to do with the visible sentence, and one or two clue-literal guesses feel absurd or score flat/MISS once you check them against the sentence, **stop trusting the clue's literal domain immediately.** Don't keep drilling that domain.

**Recovery:** ask "what is the single most obvious, most direct word a fluent writer would use in this exact sentence slot?" and guess that directly, independent of the clue. This direct-composition move is disproportionately likely to succeed outright precisely in these trap cases — a mismatched clue is itself the strongest available signal to stop analyzing the clue and just compose from the sentence.

### 4.6 Collocation gravity

Some adverbs and nouns are so habitually glued to one specific partner word ("stare fixedly," "recommend warmly," an ingredient's base material) that the habitual partner outranks true synonyms. When brainstorming, also generate "what word does this concept always appear right next to," not only "what means the same thing."

### 4.7 Invariable-plural nouns and the sibling-vs-synonym ambiguity

Nouns whose singular and plural are spelled identically have no distinct "plural sibling" to occupy a top rank, so a genuine synonym takes that slot instead — don't waste a guess "pluralizing" a noun that already ends in a way that makes singular=plural; go straight to synonym-ring expansion. More generally: **a great rank never proves "same lemma."** Hold both hypotheses — inflectional sibling, and best-synonym of a different lemma — simultaneously, and let the sentence's own grammar decide which one to actually submit.

### 4.8 Rarity and register calibration

Rarer, more literary targets sit in denser, more technical/jargon-heavy neighborhoods, and differences between high positive ranks there are noisier and less meaningful than the same gap would be for a common word. For ornate or descriptive sentences, deliberately reach for a higher vocabulary register. For rare targets, weight getting the *concept* right through reasoning over chasing small rank differences — trust grammar to finish the job once the concept is right.

---

## 5. Reading the Starting Clue

- **Reliable:** it is a genuine word sitting at a real, fixed-band distance from the true answer; the specific number within that band carries no information about the target's difficulty or rarity — don't over-read it.
- **Loosely reliable:** its broad topic/domain/register is usually a legitimate, if loose, hint about the field the answer lives in (§4.3).
- **Unreliable:** treating its literal dictionary meaning as a near-synonym to paraphrase — it frequently is not one, for the reasons above.
- **Sometimes a gift:** if the clue is obviously a conjugated or participial form sharing a root with a verb reading of the sentence, the lemma has effectively been handed to you — don't resubmit that surface form; derive and submit the grammatically required form (typically the bare infinitive) immediately.
- **Never resubmit the clue itself** — its rank is already known for free and it cannot be a new, informative guess.

---

## 6. Multi-Target Dynamics and Solve Order

Because every guess is checked against every unsolved target simultaneously, there's no per-target cost to explore broadly early on.

**Grammatical coupling:** when two blanks are grammatically bound to each other — an adjective and the noun it modifies, or an infinitive verb and its adverb (which are usually textually adjacent to each other) — their answers often surface inside each other's close neighborhoods, but **only when the pairing is a natural, stock combination** a fluent speaker would reach for. Arbitrary pairings (a generic manner adverb glued to an unrelated verb, a generic adjective glued to an unrelated noun) show little to no such cross-signal. Quick test: does the pair, said aloud, sound like an idiomatic reflex or an arbitrary combination? If idiomatic, actively cross-pollinate candidates between the two; if arbitrary, treat them independently.

**Elimination cascade:** once a target reaches rank 0, its word effectively becomes part of the visible sentence context you reason from for the remaining blanks. This is usually the single biggest context upgrade available anywhere in the puzzle — bigger than any additional clue-chasing. Immediately re-run direct-context composition (§7 Phase 1) for the unsolved targets with this new anchor in hand, and reconsider it specifically for any grammatically-coupled remaining blank.

**Ordering heuristic:** don't solve blanks in a fixed left-to-right order. Push whichever target currently shows the strongest signal (lowest rank achieved) to rank 0 first — finishing it fastest unlocks the biggest context boost for what remains. All else being roughly equal, give concrete nouns a slight priority over adjectives/verbs/adverbs as a tiebreaker, since a solved noun tends to disambiguate everything describing it — but never let this override a target that's already clearly closer to being solved.

---

## 7. Turn-by-Turn Procedure

**Phase 0 — Parse.** For every blank, fix its grammatical role, gender/number, and any coupling to another blank, using only the visible sentence (§2). Note each starting clue and rank without yet treating the clue as a synonym. Build a register/domain prior from the sentence's imagery.

**Phase 1 — Lead with direct composition.** Before analyzing any clue, for each blank generate and submit the single most obvious word a fluent French writer would place there, based purely on the sentence's plain meaning. This alone very often solves ordinary-register targets outright and is your best defense against polysemy traps (§4.5), because the sentence's plain meaning is far more trustworthy than a clue's literal domain. Only move on for blanks this doesn't immediately resolve.

**Phase 2 — Clue-anchored exploration.** For each still-open blank, generate several diagnostically different candidates: direct synonyms of the clue; other plausible members of the clue's broad category that also fit the sentence; if the clue looks bizarrely unrelated to the sentence, treat that mismatch itself as a signal to re-run direct composition instead of trusting the clue further; if the target sits on a recognizable scalar dimension, deliberately test the opposite pole as a diagnostic.

**Phase 3 — Let rank steer local search.** Use the rank tiers (§4.1) to decide your next move for each open blank. On any strong rank, sanity-check fit/polarity first (§4.2, §4.4), then either derive the correctly agreed/conjugated form of that same lemma, flip to the opposite pole, or re-express the same concept in the required part of speech — rather than abandoning a correct concept for an unrelated new one.

**Phase 4 — Cross-pollinate after every solve.** The moment any blank hits rank 0, re-read the sentence with that word filled in and re-run Phase 1 for every remaining blank, plus specifically reconsider any grammatically-coupled partner (§6).

**Phase 5 — Manage guesses; know when to pivot or stop.** Keep an explicit list of every word already tried per target (including the starting clue) and never resubmit one — the displayed clue only updates on improvement, so your own notes are the only reliable record. Apply the pivot/abandonment tests in §9. If forced to stop before solving, leave your best-scoring guess in place rather than nothing.

---

## 8. Semantic-Field Checklist for Candidate Generation

When brainstorming (Phases 1–2), work systematically through whichever of these fields the blank's concept plausibly belongs to, generating several concrete words from the *right* field before switching fields entirely:

- Manner adverbs of care/precision
- Manner adverbs of speed/pace (fast↔slow)
- Manner adverbs of volume/discretion (loud↔quiet, open↔secretive)
- Manner adverbs of emotional tone (joyful, mournful, calm, anxious, tender…)
- Manner adverbs of force/energy (vigorous↔listless)
- Manner adverbs of persistence/obstinacy
- Closed-class time/frequency adverbs (often/rarely/sometimes/always/still/already/soon/late/early/again/inside/outside/for-a-long-time/finally/henceforth…) — recall these directly, they are not built from adjectives
- Manner adverbs of movement quality (graceful↔clumsy)
- Manner adverbs of social register (polite↔curt, formal↔familiar)
- Manner adverbs of suddenness↔gradualness
- Degree/completeness adverbs
- Traditional occupation/trade nouns (artisans, rural or village roles)
- Landscape, water, and weather nouns (terrain features, precipitation types, light/time-of-day phenomena)
- Domestic or storage-space nouns (rooms, outbuildings, containers)
- Texture, material, and surface-quality adjectives
- Sound-emission verbs
- Movement/locomotion verbs
- Abstract emotional or interpersonal-state nouns

For each relevant field, recall the small *cluster* around the right concept rather than just the first word that comes to mind — the answer may be any member of that cluster, and testing two or three quickly narrows which sub-register the sentence actually wants.

---

## 9. Guess Economy and Pivot/Abandon Triggers

**Redundancy discipline.** Maintain your own tried-word list per target; never resubmit anything on it, including the starting clue.

**Soft budgeting.** No hard guess limit is confirmed; treat every guess as having real value regardless. Prefer a small number of well-reasoned candidates over scattershot volume — a handful for straightforward common-register targets, more for confirmed rare/literary ones, fewer whenever Phase 1 direct composition already lands it.

**Concrete pivot tests:**

- **Cluster exhaustion** — several guesses inside one hypothesized reading all fail to beat even the starting rank → abandon that reading; re-derive a different one from the sentence, and reconsider whether the clue reflects an unrelated sense (§4.5).
- **Plateau after a promising entry** — a strong rank stops improving across several further same-idea guesses → stop introducing new lemmas; instead enumerate the small set of agreement/conjugation variants of your current best word, test the opposite scalar pole, or reconsider the current best as a category-neighbor rather than a synonym and enumerate its category-siblings instead.
- **MISS streak** — several thematically consistent guesses all return MISS → the entire domain hypothesis is likely wrong, not just the specific words; redo Phase 0 parsing (confirm role/gender/agreement) and try a maximally different, maximally obvious direct-composition guess.
- **Suspiciously perfect but semantically wrong** — a top-tier rank whose literal meaning contradicts the sentence's evident meaning or polarity → don't treat as nearly solved; test the antonym or the correctly-typed same-concept word instead of iterating morphology on it.
- **Forced stop** — submit whatever produced the best rank so far as the final answer for that target; a good clue beats none.

---

## 10. Failure-Mode Quick Diagnosis

| Symptom | Likely cause | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Guesses matching the clue's literal meaning stay flat or MISS | Clue reflects an unrelated sense of a polysemous answer, or is a pure category hint | Stop trusting the clue's literal topic; run direct composition from the sentence |
| A rank 1–3 hit that doesn't actually fit the sentence on reflection | Antonym-on-a-shared-scale mirage | Flip polarity and guess the opposite pole directly |
| Stuck at a great rank across several *different* new lemmas | You already had the right lemma but kept abandoning it instead of fixing agreement/inflection | Stop introducing new words; enumerate the 2–4 grammatical variants of the current best lemma |
| Wasted a guess on a conjugated form for a verb-type blank | Forgot the bare-infinitive rule | Always default to infinitive for verb slots; use §3.1 to jump straight there |
| Resubmitted a word already tried | No tried-word tracking | Keep an explicit list per target |
| Many guesses spent in one plausible-but-wrong category | Category over-commitment | Apply the cluster-exhaustion pivot test (§9) |
| Solved one target but didn't leverage it for a coupled neighbor | Skipped cross-pollination | Re-run Phase 1 for remaining blanks immediately after every solve |
| Reasoning as if gender/POS/register were given directly | Confusing offline metadata with in-game visibility | Always re-derive everything from the visible sentence |
| A semantically right-seeming guess doesn't register as expected | Missing/incorrect accent, elision, or agreement ending | Proofread orthography before submitting |
| Accepted a mediocre result while cheap high-value moves were untried | Premature stop | Run Phases 1–3 fully before invoking a forced stop |
| Many guesses, many domains, never narrowing | Over-exploration without commitment | Cap exploration per hypothesis, then commit to whichever produced the best rank |

---

## 11. Generalized Worked Vignettes

**A — Direct composition beats a misleading clue.** A sentence depicts a forceful natural element steadily wearing away a hard surface, with a matching intensity adjective and a persistent action verb. One target's free clue belongs to a completely unrelated modern/technical sense of the same word and, taken literally, would send you hunting irrelevant vocabulary. Simply naming the obvious concrete noun, the obvious intensity adjective, and the obvious action verb for the scene — ignoring the clue entirely — solves all three blanks immediately.

**B — Antonym mirage plus hypernym near-miss.** A cold, wet outdoor scene needs a specific precipitation noun, a temperature adjective, and a manner adverb for how something fell. A generic "rain" guess for the noun scores very well but is one notch too broad — the scene wants the more specific subtype. Testing the "warm" pole of the temperature scale as a diagnostic returns a deceptively excellent rank purely from antonym clustering; recognizing this, you flip immediately to "cold" once the surrounding weather context confirms the scene's actual polarity. The adverb is found efficiently by testing a small cluster of low-energy movement adverbs.

**C — Severe polysemy trap resolved by abandoning the clue.** A sentence shows something freshly worked, still faintly warm at dawn, alongside a short adjective that is simultaneously a very common word for "fresh" and, in its dominant sense elsewhere, a word for "financial costs," plus a degree adverb. All three free clues, read literally, point at body parts, financial-risk vocabulary, and an unrelated idiom — none of which fit the visible scene. Because the clues are essentially nonsensical against the sentence, that mismatch is itself the signal to stop chasing them and simply compose the three most obvious words a fluent writer would use for this exact physical scene, solving all three at once.

**D — The clue hands you the lemma.** For a verb-type blank, the free clue is itself a conjugated form of the exact verb needed. Recognizing this immediately — rather than resubmitting that conjugated shape, which cannot register as solved — you strip it to the infinitive and submit that directly, closing the blank in a single guess with no further exploration required.

---

## 12. Anti-Patterns to Retire

- Treating the starting clue's dictionary meaning as a near-synonym to paraphrase.
- Treating any great rank as proof you're basically done, without a fit/polarity sanity check.
- Submitting a conjugated form for a verb-type blank instead of resolving to the grammatically required form.
- Dismissing an antonym as an obviously wrong probe rather than using it as a deliberate axis-diagnostic.
- Assuming the neighborhood you can imagine is small — high positive ranks still carry weak information, and MISS is the real "wrong branch" signal.
- Reasoning as if gender, part of speech, register, or rarity were handed to you directly instead of derived from the sentence.
- Re-trying a cosmetically different spelling of an already-tried word rather than a genuinely new candidate.
- Solving blanks strictly in their left-to-right order regardless of which one shows the strongest signal.
- Grinding a single semantic cluster well past the point where it has stopped producing improvement.

---

## 13. Calibration Checklist for the First Unseen Puzzles

Confirm or update these working assumptions as soon as live behavior lets you:

- [ ] Does the starting clue's rank still fall in the same narrow handicap band seen in training? Recalibrate expectations if not.
- [ ] Is there any visible indicator of a guess-count limit or budget?
- [ ] Does resubmitting an already-tried word produce any new observable signal?
- [ ] Are MISS and a very high numeric rank distinguished from each other, or shown identically?
- [ ] Do verb-type blanks still require the bare infinitive with no exception?
- [ ] Watch for structural surprises not covered above: plural targets, multi-word answers, two blanks of the same part of speech in one sentence, or slot types outside noun/adjective/verb-infinitive/adverb.

Adjust every confidence level in this playbook based on what you actually observe, rather than assuming prior invariants transfer perfectly.

---

## 14. One-Page Condensed Checklist

1. Parse every blank's grammatical role and agreement from the visible sentence alone before guessing anything.
2. Guess the single most obvious direct-composition word per blank first — this is your best defense against misleading clues and often solves the puzzle outright.
3. Verb-type blank → bare infinitive, always; convert any conjugated/participial lead immediately.
4. Treat the starting clue as a topic/domain hint, never as a synonym to paraphrase.
5. On any rank 1–3 hit, sanity-check literal fit and polarity before assuming you're nearly done.
6. On a scalar/bipolar target, deliberately test the opposite pole as a diagnostic when unsure of direction.
7. Cross-pollinate grammatically coupled blanks (adjective+its noun; infinitive+its adverb) when their pairing sounds like a natural, stock combination.
8. The instant any blank is solved, re-read the sentence with it filled in and re-attempt direct composition for the rest.
9. Never repeat a guess; keep your own tried-word list per target.
10. Use the pivot tests (cluster exhaustion, rank plateau, MISS streak, polarity mismatch) to know when to abandon a stale hypothesis.
11. Proofread accents, elision, and agreement before submitting.
12. Never assume gender/part-of-speech/register information is given directly — derive it from the sentence every time.
13. If forced to stop, leave your best-scoring guess as the fallback rather than nothing.
